html:
Abdurauf Fitrat (1886 to 1938) was a writer, reformer and politician from Bukhara who helped found modern Uzbek literature. He belonged to the Jadids, Muslim modernists who wanted new schools, a free press and the reform of society within Islam.

He studied in Istanbul from 1909, where he took in the ideas of the Young Turks, and wrote sharp Persian works attacking the backwardness of the Emirate of Bukhara, one of the Uzbek khanates. The best known is a debate between a Bukharan teacher and a European. After 1917 he switched to a purified Turkic language and became a champion of Uzbek national culture. He served as a minister in the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic of 1920 to 1924, then taught and wrote plays, poems and studies of Chagatai literature.

The Soviet state first used Jadids like him, then turned on them as bourgeois nationalists. He was arrested in 1937 in the Great Purge and shot in Tashkent in October 1938. He was cleared after Stalin's death, and Uzbekistan now honours him as a founder of the nation.
